_about: Hand-read key signatures, one entry per staff position, for the pages the
key-signature layer was measured on. Every value here was read off the
printed page by eye at high zoom — it is not pipeline output, and it is the
part of this benchmark that cannot be regenerated.
`fifths` is the circle-of-fifths position of the WRITTEN signature: +N for N
sharps, -N for N flats, 0 for none. `clef` is the printed clef, supplied to
the locator in component mode because the slot table is chosen by it.
Staves are keyed by ORDINAL — position within a system, top to bottom —
because that is what identifies the instrument across the systems of a page.
Every system on these pages carries the same instrumentation.

pages.work: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, Op. 67 — first movement, concert C minor
why_this_page: A degraded 19th-century print, and the page that motivated the whole
layer. It carries three different written signatures for one concert
key: 3 flats on the non-transposing parts, 1 flat on the Bb clarinet,
and none on the horns, trumpets and timpani. A naive 'all staves in a
system agree' check fails on it, and so does counting detections.

pages.work: Beethoven, Symphony No. 6, Op. 68 — first movement, concert F major
why_this_page: A second degraded print, and the one case where a transposing part
prints the OPPOSITE accidental to the rest of the page: the Bb clarinet
writes 1 sharp against everyone else's 1 flat. It is the staff both
surviving errors land on.

staves.uncertain: The flat is hard to make out at this staff's print quality; read as 1 flat because every other string part on the page prints one and the part is non-transposing.

pages.work: Bach, Well-Tempered Clavier I — E major
why_this_page: The opposite material: a clean modern engraving where the DETECTOR
fires, so it measures the path the CV locator never reaches. Four
sharps on every staff of five systems, which is what makes the
cross-page vote's job checkable by eye.

pages.work: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, Op. 67 — first movement, concert C minor (bars 430 and 452)
why_this_page: The first ground-truth page that is MID-MOVEMENT, and the first
carrying three distinct written signatures for one concert key
INCLUDING natural brass and timpani printing NONE: 3 flats on the
flutes, oboes, bassoons and every string part, 1 flat on the Bb
clarinets, and no signature at all on the horns, trumpets and timpani.
beet5-p2 has that shape at the head of the movement; this page proves
it recurs where every system merely restates the signature, which is
where the cross-page vote does its work.
It is also the page roadmap #4b cited as its evidence that key
signatures go unread, and it had NO per-staff ground truth until
2026-09-01 — which is why the +4 staves claimed for it in
benchmarks/omr-keysig-blindspot-2026-08/ were called unverifiable
there. It is the page on which the vote was caught rejecting three
CORRECT three-flat readings in favour of a reference set by two
under-counts; see benchmarks/omr-keysig-from-music-2026-09/PHASE1.md.
PROVENANCE: hand-read by eye off a 500 dpi render of the left margin.
The image the lower system was read from is kept at benchmarks/
omr-keysig-from-music-2026-09/crops/beet5_p15_sys1_headers.png so the
reading can be re-checked without re-rendering. Both systems carry the
same instrumentation and the same signatures.
The dossier DISAGREES with this print on 3 of the 11 parts: the modern
MusicXML edition data/dossiers/beethoven-sym5-mvt1.json is generated
from gives C Trumpet and Timpani written_fifths -3, where the 1870s
print gives them none. That is an EDITION difference, not an error in
either, and it is why the dossier cannot stand in for reading a page.
